name: tail
one_line: output the last part of files
plain: `tail` prints the end of a file: by default the last 10 lines. With -f it keeps the file open and prints new lines as they are added, which is how you watch a log in real time.
In incident response and defence challenges, tail -f is how you watch what an attacker is doing right now.
when: Watch a log live while you test a service or while an attack runs.
Skip a header: print from line 2 on.

examples.title: Last 10 lines
examples.explain: The newest entries of a log are at the bottom, so the end is usually the most interesting part.

examples.title: Start from a line number  (-n +N)
examples.explain: A plus sign means 'start at line N and print the rest'. -n +2 skips a header row.

examples.title: Follow a log as it grows  (-f)
examples.explain: Prints new lines as they appear, until you press Ctrl-C. Run it in a spare terminal while you try a login or send a request.

examples.title: Follow and filter
examples.explain: Shows only failed logins as they happen. --line-buffered stops grep from holding output back.

examples.title: Follow a file that gets replaced  (-F)
examples.explain: -F re-opens the file when log rotation replaces it, and keeps waiting if it does not exist yet. Use it for long watches.

examples.title: The last bytes  (-c)
examples.explain: Look at the end of a binary: data hidden after an image's end marker shows up here.

options.plain: Print the last NUM bytes; with a plus sign, start at byte NUM.
options.use: Inspecting the end of a binary or an appended payload.

options.plain: Print the last NUM lines (default 10); with a plus sign, start at line NUM.
Keep reading and print new data as the file grows. The default follows the open file even if it is renamed.
Same as --follow=name --retry: follow the file by name and keep trying if it disappears or is rotated.
Keep trying to open a file that is not accessible yet.
options.use: Following a file that will be created later.

options.plain: With -f, stop when the process with this id ends.
options.use: Watching a program's log only while it runs.

options.plain: With -f, wait about N seconds between checks.
options.use: Reducing load on a slow disk.

options.plain: With --follow=name, re-open the file after N checks without change.
Lines end with a NUL byte instead of a newline.

mistakes: Using tail -f on a file that is rotated: you stop receiving data; use -F.
Piping tail -f into another command that buffers (grep, awk): use --line-buffered or stdbuf.
tail -n 5 file is the last five lines; tail -n +5 file starts at line 5.
try: Watch auth.log in one terminal and trigger a failed ssh login in another.
Print a CSV without its header row.
Follow two logs at once with tail -f a b.
Use tail -c 100 to find data appended after the end of an image.
see_also: head(1), less(1) (press F inside less to follow), journalctl -f, multitail, grep(1), watch(1).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
